answer: Mostly the money is spent in the United States, on American-made weapons. Under the 2007 agreement Israel could spend 26.3 percent of the yearly grant at home; the 2016 agreement ends that by fiscal 2028. For fiscal 2025, $450 million of $3.3 billion was set aside for it: roughly 14 percent by our arithmetic. The US co-developed David's Sling and Arrow. US law allows arms sales only for purposes such as legitimate self-defence. A May 2024 State Department report found it reasonable to assess that US arms were used in ways inconsistent with humanitarian law; the memorandum that required it, NSM-20, was rescinded in February 2025. Senate votes to block sales failed: 17 to 19 yes in November 2024, 15 in April 2025, 36 and 40 in April 2026. A third of Americans say the US gives Israel too much military aid.

facts.text: Under the 2007 memorandum (fiscal years 2009 to 2018) Israel was explicitly permitted to spend up to 26.3 percent of the US military grant on Israeli-made equipment ('off-shore procurement'); the 2016 memorandum (fiscal years 2019 to 2028) decreases this slowly until fiscal 2024, then phases it out more steeply over its last five years, ending in fiscal 2028. The AP reported that the 2016 deal eventually requires all of the funds to be spent on American military industries.

facts.text: In fiscal 2025 Congress appropriated a $3.3 billion military grant (P.L. 119-4, per the CRS) and specified $450.3 million of it for off-shore procurement, spent in Israel: about 14 percent, by our own arithmetic (450.3 divided by 3,300). The April 2024 supplemental allowed up to $769.3 million of its $3.5 billion in grants to be spent in Israel (about 22 percent, also our arithmetic). The FY2025 act itself (P.L. 119-4, section 11206) substitutes $450,300,000 for $725,300,000 in section 7041(d); the CRS identifies that line as the off-shore procurement figure.

could_not_verify: A source from outside advocacy that says the US gets intelligence from Israel in exchange for the aid: only advocacy writers (AJC, JNS) claim it, so it is not stated as a fact.

An audited figure for the share of aid dollars spent in the United States: no source gives one. The 14 percent in the answer is our arithmetic (450.3 divided by 3,300 million), counts only off-shore procurement, and is not fuel or other items.
How much of the missile defence money is spent in the US each year: the Missile Defense Agency estimate is quoted from the CRS report only.

Fact 1 (amounts spent in Israel): the FY2025 $450.3 million and the $769.3 million of the April 2024 supplemental are in the two public laws and the CRS report; I found no two outlets or scholars reporting those amounts (the Quincy brief gives only 'about 25 percent' and the Stimson guide a fiscal 2023 figure), so the fact stays short. A person would need a Defense News, CSIS or similar report of the fiscal 2025 off-shore procurement amount. Fact 2 (where grants go) now has the CFR, Hartung's Costs of War paper and the Quincy brief, besides the CRS.
Three reliable sources for fact 4 (joint development) and fact 5 (US law): only two independent sites each.

The text of National Security Memorandum 20 and the State Department's May 2024 report: the White House and State Department pages would not load, so both are described through the CRS, Lawfare, Just Security and Al Jazeera.

Fact 8 (Gallup): the poll owner plus AP and Al Jazeera. Fact 9 (Pew's military-aid question) is a record fact: Pew's report, with The Times of Israel and JNS reporting the same question; I read the Times of Israel through its Wayback copy. Pew's party-by-age breakdown and Gallup's Republicans-by-age figures were not read.

The rescission order itself: it was not published; it is known from the Washington Post (via the CRS, Al Jazeera and a Reuters report) and Reuters could not confirm the order's existence independently, though officials said the directive was revoked. Whether the 2025 conventional arms transfer policy review replaced it was not read. I looked again for a third independent report (Politico, Axios, AP, the White House) and found only copies of the Washington Post and Reuters reports; Yahoo and Breitbart also cite the Post.
The month of Pew's survey: the cited Pew page is dated 3 October 2025 and does not state the field dates, so 'September 2025' in fact 9 is not confirmed on it.

Still short of three independent reliable sources: fact 1 (amounts spent in Israel: CRS and two public laws, no outlet reporting the amounts) and fact 6 (the rescission of NSM-20: Al Jazeera and JNS rest on one Washington Post report, so only the Post and Reuters are separate; the Arms Control Association is advocacy and is not counted). To close fact 6 a person would need the order itself or another outlet's own reporting of it. We searched for more and did not find them.

Fact 8 carries the 'record' flag for Gallup's own poll page; AP and Al Jazeera report its headline numbers (41 and 36 percent, and 65 percent of Democrats in Al Jazeera) but not the Republican and age figures, which are on the Gallup page only.
not_claimed: This card does not say the aid should continue, or end.
It does not say Israel has broken US law: the State Department said in 2024 that it had not assessed Israel to be in violation, and the May 2024 report did not reach legal findings.
It does not say Israel gives the US intelligence in return for the aid; that is claimed by advocates and not verified here.
It does not say American opinion decides policy; it reports polls only.

answer_claims.says: Mostly the money is spent in the United States, on American-made weapons.
Under the 2007 agreement Israel could spend 26.3 percent of the yearly grant at home; the 2016 agreement ends that by fiscal 2028.
For fiscal 2025, $450 million of $3.3 billion was set aside for it: roughly 14 percent by our arithmetic.
The US co-developed David's Sling and Arrow.
US law allows arms sales only for purposes such as legitimate self-defence.

A May 2024 State Department report found it reasonable to assess that US arms were used in ways inconsistent with humanitarian law; the memorandum that required it, NSM-20, was rescinded in February 2025.
Senate votes to block sales failed: 17 to 19 yes in November 2024, 15 in April 2025, 36 and 40 in April 2026.
A third of Americans say the US gives Israel too much military aid.

skeptic.notes: Round three (the last). Changed since round two and re-read: joint development has Breaking Defense and two CSIS pages besides the CFR; the CRS is cited from EveryCRSReport (450.3m, 3.3bn, 26.3 percent, 769.3m, 50 percent / $100m all present); fact 1 adds that P.L. 119-4 section 11206 substitutes $450,300,000 for $725,300,000 (the law text is on its page; the CRS says that line is off-shore procurement); the survey date is now 'the report of 3 October 2025'. Senate counts checked against senate.gov: S.J.Res. 111 18-79, 113 19-78, 115 17-80 (November 2024), S.J.Res. 26 15-83 and 33 15-82 (April 2025), S.J.Res. 138 36-63 and 32 40-59 (April 2026); I added the other two November 2024 votes to the fact because the answer's '18' hid them. Percentages recomputed: 450.3/3,300 = 13.6, 769.3/3,500 = 22.0, both labelled our arithmetic. Applied the 'record' flag to fact 7 (roll calls, with Al Jazeera, JTA and Roll Call reporting them) and fact 8 (Gallup's page, with AP and Al Jazeera reporting its headline). Not flagged: fact 1 (law text and CRS have no two outlets reporting the same amounts), fact 2, fact 6, fact 9. Fact 6: AL Jazeera and JNS only repeat the Washington Post, so I declared them one source: two independent sources remain (Post, Reuters). Contested now quotes Senator Graham (Jewish Insider). Still blocking verified: fact 1 (appropriated amounts spent in Israel), fact 2 (where grants go), fact 6 (rescission), fact 9 (Pew). Person: fact 1 needs two outlets or scholars reporting the FY2025 $450.3m off-shore procurement and the $769.3m (e.g. a CRS-citing think tank like CSIS or CFR on OSP amounts, or Defense News); fact 2 a second source that most FMF is spent on US equipment (e.g. DSCA or Brookings); fact 6 a third independent report of the rescission, ideally the White House or NSC document or Politico/Axios; fact 9 two outlets reporting Pew's October 2025 military-aid question, or the question's topline.
